passage: Rain tapped the kitchen window in Valencia. Santiago, five, pushed his soup around until his big sister Layla pulled a sock over her ear and held it like a phone. "Hello? Is this the soup? The soup is too hot, he says." Santiago snorted. Layla answered the sock in a deep voice: "Blub blub, I am a noodle." Santiago laughed so hard he slid off his chair. From the floor he shouted, "Spoonapotamus! A spoon that is a hippo!" and laughed at his own word all over again.

qa.q: What did Layla pull over her ear?
qa.a: A sock, which she held like a phone.

qa.q: What was Santiago feeling when he slid off his chair?
qa.a: He was delighted; the talking sock and the noodle voice struck him as so silly that he laughed until he fell.

qa.q: How could Layla use Santiago's love of silly words at the next dull meal?
qa.a: She could start a made-up word game, letting him invent names like spoonapotamus for the food and cutlery.

qa.q: How might Layla see her little brother's new word?
qa.a: She would probably find it funny and be pleased that her joke got him inventing his own nonsense.

grounding: A five-year-old laughs at a sister's absurd sock phone and then invents a silly word of his own.

passage: Diwali week at Little Steps Playschool. Kiran Ma'am had strung paper lamps across the room, and one fell right onto her head. She froze, looked up with crossed eyes and said, "Oh no. The lamp has chosen me. I am the lamp queen now." Sarita squealed. Kiran Ma'am bowed slowly and the lamp slipped over one eye. "And the lamp queen says... moo!" Sarita laughed until she hiccuped. For the rest of the morning, every time anyone said "lamp," she whispered "moo" and giggled.

qa.q: What fell onto Kiran Ma'am's head?
qa.a: One of the paper lamps strung across the room.

qa.q: Why did Sarita keep whispering "moo" all morning?
qa.a: She was still tickled by the silly surprise of a lamp queen who mooed, and repeating it let her enjoy the joke again. 😊

qa.q: What did Kiran Ma'am's reaction to the fallen lamp do well for the class?
qa.a: By turning an accident into a silly act instead of getting flustered, she gave the children a safe, shared joke.

qa.q: What would change if Kiran Ma'am had just taken the lamp off and carried on?
qa.a: Sarita would probably have noticed the fall but missed the fun; the absurd lamp queen and her moo made it funny.

grounding: A preschooler finds a teacher's absurd lamp-queen act hilarious during Diwali week.

passage: I'm Shankar, and I live across the lane from Thomas's family. It was the first heavy monsoon week. I saw Thomas, maybe five, standing on his porch while his grandmother tied a plastic raincoat on their fat brown dog. The dog sat there, very serious, hood over one ear. Thomas pointed and laughed so hard he had to hold the railing. Then he put his own bucket on his head and marched around the dog saying, "Now we're both raincoats!" I can't know what he was thinking, but I laughed too.

qa.q: What did Thomas put on his own head?
qa.a: His bucket.

qa.q: What does Thomas holding the railing while laughing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was overjoyed by the odd sight of a serious dog in a raincoat, laughing so hard he had to steady himself.

qa.q: How could Thomas's grandmother join in his fun?
qa.a: She could play along with the silly idea, perhaps asking the raincoat dog and the bucket boy to march together.

qa.q: Why does Shankar say, "I can't know what he was thinking"?
qa.a: Shankar is only watching from across the lane, so Shankar can see the laughter but can only guess what exactly amused Thomas.

grounding: A neighbour sees a young boy laugh at a dog in a raincoat and then clown with a bucket in the monsoon.

passage: Behind the school in Barmer stood the headman's guava tree, heavy with fruit. Kunal, five, walked under it slowly and kept his hands in his pockets. "Why don't you take one?" asked his cousin. "Manjula Aaji said if I don't touch the tree all week, she'll give me gud on Sunday," Kunal said. "And the headman shouts." He looked up at a yellow guava and swallowed. "A big piece of gud," he said again, to himself, and walked faster.

qa.q: What did Manjula Aaji promise Kunal?
qa.a: She said she would give him gud on Sunday if he didn't touch the tree all week.

qa.q: What is Kunal feeling as he looks up at the yellow guava and swallows?
qa.a: He is tempted by the fruit, but the thought of the reward and the headman shouting keeps him walking.

qa.q: How could Manjula Aaji help Kunal begin to think beyond the reward?
qa.a: She could ask him how the headman might feel if his guavas went missing, so he starts to think about other people too.

qa.q: How does Kunal's cousin see the tree?
qa.a: The cousin sees easy fruit and seems puzzled that Kunal won't take one.

grounding: A small boy leaves a tree's fruit alone only to earn jaggery and avoid being shouted at.

passage: December in Durban was hot, and the Christmas biscuits sat on the table under a cloth. "Aren't you having one?" Aiko asked. Lindiwe shook her head hard. "Mama said if I wait until after lunch, I get a star on my chart." "Is it naughty to take one?" Lindiwe thought. "It's naughty because then you don't get the star. And no cartoon after." She sat on her hands. "Five stars and I get the red bucket." Aiko nodded slowly and sat on her hands too.

qa.q: Where were the Christmas biscuits?
qa.a: On the table under a cloth.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling as she sat on her hands?
qa.a: She was tempted, but eager to earn the star and worried about losing her cartoon.

qa.q: How could Mama build on Lindiwe's waiting?
qa.a: Mama could praise the waiting and also talk about sharing the biscuits fairly, so the reason grows beyond stars.

qa.q: Why might Aiko have copied Lindiwe?
qa.a: Aiko seemed to accept Lindiwe's reasoning that taking a biscuit was bad because of the lost star.

grounding: A five-year-old explains that taking a biscuit is naughty because it costs her a star and a cartoon.

passage: The Eid holiday was coming, and Jatin Sir's kindergarten class lined up for the sweet sevaiyan a parent had sent. Zainab stood very straight at the back. The boy in front of her tried to push forward. "Don't!" Zainab hissed. "Jatin Sir said whoever stands nicely gets the star badge." "So?" "And pushers sit on the bench." The boy stepped back. When Jatin Sir walked past and pinned a badge on her kurta, Zainab glowed and touched it the whole time she ate.

qa.q: What did Jatin Sir pin on Zainab's kurta?
qa.a: A star badge.

qa.q: How can you tell Zainab felt proud of the badge?
qa.a: She glowed and kept touching it while she ate.

qa.q: How could Jatin Sir help the children see a reason beyond badges for waiting in line?
qa.a: He could ask them how it feels when someone pushes in front, so fairness also matters.

qa.q: What would change for the boy if there were no bench and no badge?
qa.a: He might have kept pushing, since Zainab's warning worked only by naming the reward and the punishment.

grounding: A kindergartner stands in line nicely for a badge and to avoid the bench.

passage: The bus was stuck in traffic outside Pune for over an hour. Simran had one small chocolate left, the one she'd saved all day. Her cousin Chaitanya, three, had cried himself hoarse and was now kicking the seat. "Hungry," he whimpered. Simran looked at the chocolate. She really wanted all of it. She broke it, made the two halves nearly equal, then gave him the slightly bigger one. Chaitanya went quiet, chocolate on his chin. Simran nibbled her half very slowly to make it last.

qa.q: How long was the bus stuck in traffic?
qa.a: For over an hour.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she looked at the chocolate?
qa.a: She was torn; she really wanted it all but could see how hungry and upset Chaitanya was.

qa.q: What could an adult on the bus say to Simran afterwards?
qa.a: They could thank her warmly for sharing the chocolate she had saved, noticing that it was hard to give up.

qa.q: How was Chaitanya affected by Simran's choice?
qa.a: The hungry little boy calmed down and stopped crying once he had the chocolate.

grounding: A five-year-old shares her only chocolate with a crying cousin on a delayed bus despite wanting it herself.

passage: Holi morning in the Andheri colony. Pallavi had a brand-new water pistol, green and shiny. Ira from the second floor had nothing but her hands, and she stood near the gate watching the other kids splash. Pallavi squirted one more stream at the wall. Then she walked over and held the pistol out. "Your turn. Five squirts, then mine." Ira's face lit up. Pallavi counted each squirt out loud, fists clenched, then took it back and handed it again after her own five.

qa.q: What colour was Pallavi's water pistol?
qa.a: Green and shiny.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling while Ira had her turn?
qa.a: She felt reluctant and a little anxious about her new toy, clenching her fists and counting every squirt out loud.

qa.q: What could a parent watching from the balcony say to Pallavi?
qa.a: They could tell her it was kind to share her new toy, and that taking turns looked like fun for both girls.

qa.q: What was Holi morning like for Ira before and after Pallavi came over?
qa.a: At first Ira felt left out, watching from the gate; then her face lit up as she joined the play.

grounding: A child shares her new water pistol with a girl who has none during Holi, though she wants to keep using it.

passage:
On Sankranti evening, Abhinav held the last sesame chikki.
"Bhaiya, give!" said Jagdish, reaching.
"It's mine. I saved it."
"I didn't get one." Jagdish's lip shook.
Dadaji looked up from the kite string. "Hmm. What will you do?"
Abhinav held the chikki tighter. "I want it."
"I know."
Abhinav snapped it in two. "Here. But mine's the bigger one."
Jagdish bit his half. "Crunchy!"
Abhinav chewed and grinned. "Tomorrow you share your kite."
"Deal!"

qa.q: What was Dadaji doing when he looked up?
qa.a: He was working on the kite string.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he said, "I want it"?
qa.a: He felt possessive and reluctant; he had saved the chikki and wanted it for himself.

qa.q: What worked about Dadaji's question "What will you do?"
qa.a: It let Abhinav make the choice himself, so the sharing came from him rather than an order.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel when Abhinav refused at first, and then when he got his half?
qa.a: Jagdish looked close to tears at first, then seemed happy with the crunchy half.

grounding: A young boy splits his last chikki with a younger child though he wanted it, after a grandfather asks what he'll do.

passage: The sweet shop in Lajpat Nagar smelled of hot sugar. Parveen, five, pressed her nose to the glass. "One jalebi now," said Irawati Khala, "or two after dinner if you wait. Your choice." Parveen looked at the orange spirals for a long time. "Two," she said. Then she turned her back to the counter and hummed loudly all the way home. At dinner she ate fast and asked, "Now?" Khala laughed and put two jalebis on her plate.

qa.q: What choice did Irawati Khala give Parveen?
qa.a: One jalebi now, or two after dinner if she waited.

qa.q: Why did Parveen turn her back to the counter and hum loudly?
qa.a: She was tempted by the jalebis and was keeping herself from looking at them so she could wait for two.

qa.q: What did Irawati Khala do that made it easier for Parveen to wait?
qa.a: She made the choice clear and let Parveen choose, then kept her word after dinner.

qa.q: What would change if Irawati Khala had forgotten her promise at dinner?
qa.a: Parveen would likely feel let down and be less willing to wait next time.

grounding: A five-year-old turns away and hums to resist one jalebi now for two after dinner.

passage:
On Diwali evening, Aadhya held the box of phuljhadis.
"Mumma, light one now! Please!"
"It's still light out," said Himani. "If you wait till it's dark and Papa is home, we can light four together."
"Four?"
"Four. But not one now."
Aadhya put the box on the table. She picked it up. She put it down again. "I'll count the diyas," she said, and walked away from the box to count.
Later, in the dark, she held the fourth sparkler high. "It was worth it!"

qa.q: How many sparklers did Himani promise if Aadhya waited?
qa.a: Four, once it was dark and Papa was home.

qa.q: What does Aadhya picking up the box and putting it down again suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a strong pull to light one right away and was struggling to wait.

qa.q: Which strategy helped Aadhya wait?
qa.a: She moved away from the box and busied herself counting diyas.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when Aadhya said, "It was worth it"?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and glad that her daughter managed to wait. 🙂

grounding: A young girl distracts herself on Diwali to wait for four sparklers instead of one straight away.

passage: Class KG-B, Christmas party, 20 December. Note by Kavitha, class teacher. I offered each child a slice of plum cake now, or a whole small cake to decorate and take home after the carol practice. Jeevan chose to wait. During practice he kept looking at the cake tray, then deliberately sat facing the window. Twice he said, "I'm waiting, I'm waiting," to himself. When practice ended he was first to the table and spent a long time with the icing. I told his father at pickup, and I'll give him the tray-carrying job tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do during practice to keep from looking at the tray?
qa.a: He deliberately sat facing the window.

qa.q: What does Jeevan saying "I'm waiting, I'm waiting" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt tempted and was reminding himself of his goal to stay patient.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do after noticing Jeevan's effort?
qa.a: She told his father at pickup and planned to give him the tray-carrying job.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's father feel hearing about the plum cake?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud that his son chose to wait for the bigger reward.

grounding: A teacher's note records a kindergartner waiting through carol practice for a cake to decorate instead of a slice now.

passage: In the Kudal anganwadi, the children sat on a mat. Didi held up a picture of a cow. "Who knows what it gives us?" Dilnaz shouted "Milk!" before anyone else, then banged the floor. Salma raised her hand high and wiggled her fingers, lips pressed shut. Didi smiled at her. "Salma?" "Milk and curd," Salma said. Dilnaz shouted again. Didi said gently, "Dilnaz, hand up, like Salma." Dilnaz scowled, then put up her hand, just a little.

qa.q: What picture did Didi hold up?
qa.a: A picture of a cow.

qa.q: What does Salma pressing her lips shut while raising her hand suggest?
qa.a: She was eager to answer but wanted to follow the rule, so she was holding the words in.

qa.q: How did Didi help Dilnaz without scolding?
qa.a: She calmly reminded Dilnaz to raise her hand, pointing to Salma as an example.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Salma was chosen?
qa.a: She may have felt annoyed and a bit left out, since she had already shouted the answer.

grounding: In a village anganwadi, one child raises her hand patiently while another shouts out.

passage: Snow had closed the playground, so Class R stayed in for circle time in Leeds. Mrs Clarke passed round the talking stone. "Only the one holding it speaks." Hiroshi held it carefully and told everyone about his snowman. Abebe called out, "Mine was bigger!" and rolled onto his back, kicking. "Abebe, it's Hiroshi's turn." Abebe kicked harder. Mrs Clarke moved beside him and said quietly, "The stone comes to you next." Abebe sat up, arms folded, and waited, staring at the stone.

qa.q: What did Mrs Clarke pass round at circle time?
qa.a: The talking stone.

qa.q: What does Abebe kicking harder after being reminded suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt frustrated and impatient about waiting for his turn to share.

qa.q: What did Mrs Clarke do that helped Abebe settle?
qa.a: She moved close, spoke quietly, and told him he would have the stone next.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi have felt when Abebe called out during his turn?
qa.a: Hiroshi may have felt interrupted, perhaps a little hurt that his snowman story was cut off.

grounding: On a snowy day, one reception child takes his turn with a talking stone while another calls out and kicks.

passage: The Pongal week kolams were chalked on the classroom floor. Kashish sat still on the mat with her hands folded. Lakshmi would not sit. She threw a crayon and yelled, "No story!" The teacher, Mrs Pillai, knelt to her level. "You can stand by the window and listen, or sit next to Kashish." Lakshmi stamped once, then sat beside Kashish, not quite touching the mat. By the end of the story she was leaning on Kashish's arm, listening.

qa.q: What had been chalked on the classroom floor?
qa.a: The Pongal week kolams.

qa.q: Why might Lakshmi have yelled "No story!" and thrown a crayon?
qa.a: She may have felt unsettled or cross about having to sit still, and showed it by refusing.

qa.q: What worked in Mrs Pillai's response?
qa.a: She knelt to Lakshmi's level and offered two acceptable choices instead of a battle.

qa.q: How might Kashish have experienced Lakshmi's outburst and then leaning on her?
qa.a: Kashish may have felt startled at first, then trusted, as Lakshmi calmed down beside her.

grounding: During Pongal week, one child sits still while another throws a crayon, then settles when offered choices.

passage: The lift in the Malad building was broken again, so Devika climbed the stairs with her mother. On the third floor, Noor Aunty was watering her plants. Devika stopped, joined her palms and said, "Namaste, Noor Aunty." Noor Aunty smiled and began telling a long story about her tulsi plant. Devika's legs were tired, but she stood still and listened with her eyes on Noor Aunty's face. When the story ended, she said, "Thank you, Aunty. Bye-bye!"

qa.q: What was Noor Aunty doing on the third floor?
qa.a: She was watering her plants.

qa.q: What does Devika standing still despite tired legs suggest?
qa.a: She felt respectful toward Noor Aunty and wanted to be polite, even though she was tired.

qa.q: How could Devika's mother encourage this manner?
qa.a: She could tell Devika later that she noticed her careful listening and polite greeting.

qa.q: How might Noor Aunty feel about Devika's greeting and listening?
qa.a: She would likely feel valued and pleased that a small child listened to her story. 😊

grounding: A young girl greets an elderly neighbour politely and listens to her story despite being tired.

passage:
On Eid morning, Manoj stood at Noor Nani's door with his father.
"Say it like I taught you," Papa whispered.
"Eid Mubarak, Nani," Manoj said, bowing his head.
"Eid Mubarak, beta! Come, sit."
Noor Nani told them about the first Eid in her old house. Manoj wanted to look at the sweets, but he kept his eyes on her.
"And then the goat ran into the kitchen!"
Manoj giggled. "Then what, Nani?"
"Such a good listener," she said, and passed him the sheer khurma.

qa.q: What greeting did Manoj say at the door?
qa.a: "Eid Mubarak, Nani."

qa.q: What does Manoj asking "Then what, Nani?" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows he was genuinely curious and enjoying her story, not only being polite.

qa.q: What did Papa do that helped Manoj know how to behave?
qa.a: He taught Manoj the greeting beforehand and quietly reminded him at the door.

qa.q: How did Noor Nani respond to Manoj's attention?
qa.a: She was pleased, calling him a good listener and passing him the sheer khurma.

grounding: On Eid, a young boy greets an elderly neighbour respectfully and listens to her story.

passage: Grandparents' Day, a crisp winter morning in January. Note by Karthik, class teacher, UKG. When the visiting grandparents came in, Raghav went to the door without being asked, greeted Mrs Nair's grandfather with "Vanakkam, Thatha," and offered him the big chair. During the talk about old toys, Raghav sat still and kept his voice low when he asked a question. At the end he said thank you twice. I praised him in front of the class and asked him to help welcome visitors next month.

qa.q: What did Raghav offer the visiting grandfather?
qa.a: The big chair.

qa.q: What might Raghav have been feeling when he greeted the visitor without being asked?
qa.a: He likely felt eager and proud to welcome the grandparents and show good manners.

qa.q: What did Karthik do after noticing Raghav's behaviour?
qa.a: He praised Raghav in front of the class and asked him to help welcome visitors next month.

qa.q: How might the visiting grandfather have felt about Raghav's greeting?
qa.a: He likely felt welcomed and respected by the small boy's warm greeting and care. 🙏

grounding: A teacher's note records a young boy greeting visiting grandparents politely and listening quietly.

passage:
Monday: At the end of play, Arohi left crayons all over the floor of the classroom. Sarita Ma'am picked them up while Arohi ran to the door.
Wednesday: Sarita Ma'am gave her a small basket. "This is the crayon home. Can you help me?" Arohi dropped them in one by one, humming.
The next Monday: Before anyone asked, Arohi put the caps back on the markers, filled the basket and watered the class plant. "I'm the helper!" she told her mother at pickup.

qa.q: What did Sarita Ma'am give Arohi on Wednesday?
qa.a: A small basket for the crayons.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when she told her mother, "I'm the helper!"?
qa.a: She felt proud and pleased with her new job.

qa.q: What worked in Sarita Ma'am's approach?
qa.a: She made tidying a small, clear job with a special basket and asked for help instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might Arohi's mother feel hearing "I'm the helper!"?
qa.a: She would likely feel happy and proud that her daughter is taking responsibility at school.

grounding: Across a week, a young girl goes from leaving crayons out to tidying and watering the class plant on her own.

passage: The monsoon had knocked out the power in Guwahati, and everything smelled damp. Hemant lit a candle and began folding the washing he'd dried indoors. Binita, five, came to help. "Socks are my job," she said. She paired them by feel in the dim light, lining up the small ones. Then she saw the muddy shoes by the door. She carried them to the mat outside and set them in a row. "No mud inside, Papa." Hemant laughed. "Our house boss."

qa.q: What was Hemant doing by candlelight?
qa.a: Folding the washing he'd dried indoors.

qa.q: What does Binita saying "Socks are my job" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud and responsible, happy to have her own part in the chores.

qa.q: How could Hemant keep encouraging Binita's help?
qa.a: He could keep giving her small jobs like the socks and thank her for noticing the muddy shoes.

qa.q: How might the dark, damp evening feel different for Hemant because of Binita's help?
qa.a: The chores would feel lighter and more fun, and he enjoys his daughter's care for the house. 😊

grounding: During a monsoon power cut, a small girl pairs socks and moves muddy shoes out to keep the house clean.

passage: A week before Diwali, the whole flat in Chembur smelled of wet cloth. Kamal Chacha was scrubbing the high shelves. Jeevan, five, got a damp rag of his own. "I'll do the low ones," he said. He wiped each shelf slowly, putting the small brass lamps back exactly where they were. Then he swept the dust from under the sofa into a pile. "Look, Chacha!" Kamal Chacha peered down. "Very neat. Now carry it to the bin with me."

qa.q: What was Kamal Chacha scrubbing?
qa.a: The high shelves.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he called, "Look, Chacha!"?
qa.a: He felt proud of his work and eager to show it.

qa.q: What did Kamal Chacha do that made Jeevan's help work?
qa.a: He let Jeevan take the low shelves and praised the neat job, then did the last step together.

qa.q: How might the Diwali cleaning feel for Kamal Chacha with Jeevan helping?
qa.a: It would feel less of a chore and more of a shared job with his young nephew.

grounding: A five-year-old helps with Diwali cleaning by wiping low shelves and sweeping dust.

passage:
Reading notes, Saturday. Tutor: Gurpreet.
Anjali, 7, still guesses words from the first letter. Today I put three cards on the table: s, h and ip. She sounded them slowly, "sss... h... ip," frowning. I showed her that s and h together make "sh." She tried again: "sh... ip. Ship!" She looked up, surprised. Then she read "shop" and "fish" on her own, pointing at each sound with her finger. When a word got hard she sighed and wanted to stop, so we took a short break. Next week: more sh words, and a short boat story she can read to her little brother.

qa.q: What three cards did Gurpreet put on the table?
qa.a: The cards s, h and ip.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when she read "Ship!"?
qa.a: She was surprised and pleased that the sounds joined into a real word.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do when a word got hard?
qa.a: Gurpreet noticed her sigh and took a short break with her.

qa.q: How might Anjali's little brother feel when she reads the boat story to him?
qa.a: He would likely enjoy being read to and may admire his sister's new skill.

grounding: A tutor's note records a seven-year-old learning to blend sounds and read short words.

passage:
Tuesday night. Trisha's diary.
Today I read the whole of chapter three to Lakshmi without stopping once! Not even on "mysterious." Last month I used to get stuck on every long word and Lakshmi would get bored and roll away. Tonight she listened till the end and asked why the girl in the story hid the key. I said it was because she was scared the grown-ups would blame her brother. I didn't read that anywhere, I just knew from the story. That felt like real reading. Lakshmi fell asleep before chapter four. Tomorrow!

qa.q: Which long word did Trisha read without getting stuck?
qa.a: "Mysterious."

qa.q: How did Trisha feel about understanding why the girl hid the key?
qa.a: Trisha felt proud and excited, sensing that working out the reason meant real reading.

qa.q: How could Trisha keep building on tonight's reading?
qa.a: Trisha could keep reading a chapter to Lakshmi each night and talking about why the characters do things.

qa.q: How has reading time changed for Lakshmi since last month?
qa.a: Last month Lakshmi got bored and rolled away; now she listens to the end and asks questions.

grounding: A child's diary shows new reading fluency and understanding of a story's hidden reason.

passage: In the village of Kumily, the seed packets had come with new pictures and words. Sahil's grandmother held one out. "What does it say, kanna? My eyes are no good." Sahil, eight, traced the letters with his thumb. "Plant... in... rows. Water... every... morning." He read it again faster, then looked up. "It says to put them in rows, Ammachi, and water them in the morning, not the evening." His teacher, Maria Miss, had been making them read signboards all month. Ammachi laughed. "So you're my reader now." Sahil grinned and ran to get the watering can.

qa.q: What did the seed packet say to do?
qa.a: Plant in rows and water every morning.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when Ammachi called him her reader?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, and eager to help.

qa.q: What could Sahil do to keep improving his reading at home?
qa.a: He could read more everyday things aloud, like packets and signs, for his grandmother.

qa.q: How might Ammachi feel about Sahil's reading?
qa.a: She likely feels pleased and relieved to have a grandson who can now read for her. 🙂

grounding: A village boy sounds out and then fluently reads a seed packet for his grandmother.

passage: Sonali Ma'am poured tamarind seeds onto each desk. "Make four groups of three." Madhav counted them into small piles, lips moving. "Now, how many altogether?" He started counting one by one again. "Wait," he said. "Three, six, nine, twelve!" He looked up. "It's four times three. It's the same thing!" Sonali Ma'am smiled. "Show me five groups of two." Madhav made them fast and said, "Ten," without counting. He sat back, grinning, and pushed his seeds into a new pattern to try six times four.

qa.q: What did Sonali Ma'am pour onto each desk?
qa.a: Tamarind seeds.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when he said, "It's the same thing!"?
qa.a: He was excited, surprised and proud at seeing that counting groups and multiplying were connected.

qa.q: How could Sonali Ma'am build on Madhav's discovery?
qa.a: She could give him larger groups or ask him to draw arrays to link the seeds to written multiplication.

qa.q: How might a classmate still counting one by one see Madhav's quick answer?
qa.a: A classmate might feel curious or a little behind and want to know his trick.

grounding: A child moves from counting seeds one by one to understanding multiplication as groups.

passage: I'm Ishita, Hrithik's older sister. On Sunday Mummy made one big paratha and said Hrithik and I had to share it with Papa and her. Hrithik, who's nine, cut it in half, then stopped. "No, four people," he said, and cut each half again. "So each is one quarter." Then he picked up a piece and said, "If I give you my quarter, you get two quarters, that's half!" I don't know what went on in his head, but last month he got mixed up with fractions. Today he looked so sure.

qa.q: How many people shared the paratha?
qa.a: Four people: Hrithik, Ishita, Papa and Mummy.

qa.q: What might Hrithik have felt when he worked out that two quarters make a half?
qa.a: He likely felt confident and pleased to finally understand fractions.

qa.q: How could Ishita support Hrithik's new understanding?
qa.a: Ishita could make more everyday fraction puzzles with food or paper for him to solve.

qa.q: How does Ishita see her brother's change?
qa.a: Ishita sees he has improved since last month, though she can't be sure what he was thinking.

grounding: An older sister watches her brother grasp quarters and halves by sharing a paratha.

passage:
First week: Santosh, eight, counted on his fingers to do 15 minus 7 and kept losing track. His cousin Suraj drew a number line on the back of an envelope.
Two weeks later: Santosh jumped back seven on the line, then said, "Or take away five, then two more." He checked with his fingers and grinned.
A month later: Suraj and Santosh were sharing out 24 marbles among four friends. Santosh said, "Six each," before Suraj finished counting. "How?" "Four sixes are twenty-four. Easy!" Suraj nodded, impressed.

qa.q: What did Suraj draw the number line on?
qa.a: The back of an envelope.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he grinned after checking with his fingers?
qa.a: He felt pleased and confident that his new method gave the right answer.

qa.q: What helped Santosh move beyond counting on his fingers?
qa.a: Suraj gave him a number line, which let him see jumps and break numbers into easier parts.

qa.q: How does Suraj see Santosh's progress by the end?
qa.a: Suraj is impressed that Santosh can now divide marbles quickly using multiplication.

grounding: Over a month, a boy moves from finger-counting to using number lines and multiplication.

passage: The school lab in Hubballi smelled of vinegar. Kunal Sir said: "Listen carefully. Put two spoons of soda in the cup. Add a little vinegar. Watch the bubbles. Then write what you saw." He said it only once. Kishore, ten, whispered the steps under his breath, "soda, vinegar, watch, write," tapping one finger for each. Last term he always forgot the last step. Today he did all four in order and wrote "fizz, then foam, then quiet." He looked up at Kunal Sir, smiling.

qa.q: How many spoons of soda were they told to put in the cup?
qa.a: Two spoons.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he looked up at Kunal Sir?
qa.a: He felt proud and satisfied at completing all four steps correctly.

qa.q: What strategy helped Kishore remember the steps?
qa.a: He whispered the steps to himself and tapped a finger for each one.

qa.q: How might Kunal Sir see Kishore's improvement since last term?
qa.a: He would likely be pleased to see Kishore remember all the steps without reminders.

grounding: A ten-year-old uses a whispered, finger-tap method to hold four lab steps in mind.

passage: I'm Leela. On Saturday I watched my brother Akash, eleven, make lemon rice for the first time. Amma read the steps once from the old notebook: rinse the rice, heat the oil, add mustard seeds, then the curry leaves, then the lemon at the very end. Last year he'd forget halfway and ask again. This time he said them back to Amma first, then went step by step without looking at the notebook. Only once did he pause, spoon in the air, eyes closed, before reaching for the curry leaves. I don't know what he was thinking, but it tasted right.

qa.q: What was added at the very end?
qa.a: The lemon.

qa.q: What does Akash pausing with eyes closed suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was concentrating hard, perhaps a little unsure, trying to remember the next step.

qa.q: What helped Akash follow the recipe this time?
qa.a: He said the steps back to Amma first, which helped him hold them in mind.

qa.q: How does Leela see her brother's cooking compared with last year?
qa.a: Leela notices he no longer forgets halfway and can do it without asking again.

grounding: A sister watches her brother follow a multi-step recipe from memory.

passage:
Week 1: At football practice, Coach Rekha said, "Dribble to the cone, pass to Kamal, run to the flag, then back." Kamal, nine, got to the cone and stopped, scratching his head. "What next?"
Week 3: Rekha gave the steps again. Kamal said them back, "cone, pass, flag, back," and did three of the four before looking around.
Week 6: Rekha smiled and said she was adding a fifth step: a shot at goal. Kamal listened, nodded, and did all five without stopping, then jogged back, beaming. "I didn't forget anything!"

qa.q: How many steps did Kamal do in Week 6?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when he said, "I didn't forget anything!"?
qa.a: He felt proud and delighted with himself.

qa.q: What helped Kamal get better at following the drill?
qa.a: Saying the steps back to himself and practising the same drill over weeks.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel about Kamal's progress by Week 6?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and encouraged to see him manage longer instructions.

grounding: Over six weeks, a nine-year-old gets better at following a multi-step football drill.
